meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('something') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: I want to show you something.

examples.text: И ещё кое-что. Эдуард Владимирович просил передать привет.
examples.trans: And one more thing. Eduard Vladimirovich asked us to pass on his regards.

meanings.note: once; что скажешь? = what do you say?
Secondary conversational sense ('tell me / tell us') (polite request) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: + past tense: 'чтобы свидетели были'
Secondary conversational sense ('in order to') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: + instrumental: стал сентиментальным
Secondary conversational sense ('to start (doing)') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты слишком сентиментальным стал. А лидер должен быть жёстким.
examples.trans: You've become too sentimental. And a leader has to be tough.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Common feminine noun meaning 'wife' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I'm with my wife this evening.

examples.text: Но вечером я обещал быть с женой.
examples.trans: But I promised to be with my wife this evening.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: сойти с ума = to go mad, lose one's mind

examples.text: Позвонить Третьякову? Я что, с ума сошёл?
examples.trans: Call Tretyakov? What, have I lost my mind?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ойти'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go mad (with с ума), come down'.

examples.trans: What, have I lost my mind?

examples.text: Позвонить Третьякову? Я что, с ума сошёл?
examples.trans: Call Tretyakov? What, have I lost my mind?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('whether') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
colloquial tag at the end of a question

examples.text: Вы что, меня покупаете, что ли?
examples.trans: What, are you buying me or something?
I don't know whether he is home.

meanings.note: + prepositional; об before a vowel: об этом

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: слава богу = thank God (literally 'glory to God')

examples.text: О, наконец тепло! Слава богу. Сейчас ещё чай сделаю.
examples.trans: Oh, it's warm at last! Thank goodness. Now I'll make some tea too.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to take', forming an aspectual pair with 'взять'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
'брать' alone often means this, in talk about officials

examples.trans: We have to take all the money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to speak, to talk') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: movement by foot or figurative action

examples.text: Надо следить за каждым шагом соперника.
examples.trans: We must monitor every step of the rival.

examples.text: Надо следить за каждым шагом кандидата.
examples.trans: We must monitor every step of the candidate.

meanings.note: mostly in set phrases: иметь совесть, иметь право = to have the right; everyday 'I have' is у меня есть

examples.trans: You have the right to remain silent.

examples.text: Нина, имей совесть! Я вчера ради вас всё сделал.
examples.trans: Nina, have a heart! Yesterday I did everything for you.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: иметь в виду = to mean, to have in mind
иметь в виду = to mean, to have in mind

examples.text: Из окна красивый вид на парк.
examples.trans: There is a nice view of the park from the window.

examples.text: Что вы имеете в виду, Клавдия Викторовна?
examples.trans: What do you mean, Klavdia Viktorovna?

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'acquaintance', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Костя, я имела в виду знакомство с родителями.
examples.trans: Kostya, I meant meeting the parents.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'parents' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: My parents live in the country.

examples.text: Я здесь работаю. Только, пожалуйста, родителям не говорите.
examples.trans: I work here. Just please don't tell my parents.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'along' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('along, around') (+ dative) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('by (phone)') ('по телефону') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Это Аракелян. Я по поводу торгового центра.
examples.trans: It's Arakelyan. I'm calling about the shopping centre.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'plan' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The mayor came up with a new plan.

examples.text: Но мэр придумал новый план. Сосед мэра теперь пойдёт в мэры.
examples.trans: But the mayor came up with a new plan. The mayor's neighbour will now run for mayor.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: softens a request: только не сердись = just don't be angry
+ accusative: через неделю = in a week
Secondary conversational sense ('through, across') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нормально? Она через неделю снова потечёт!
examples.trans: Fine? It'll be leaking again in a week!

meanings.note: after 2, 3, 4: года; after 5 and more: лет

examples.trans: I've been working here for four years.

examples.text: Это было давно, тридцать лет назад.
examples.trans: That was long ago, thirty years back.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: declines like какой: какая-то, какое-то, какие-то

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'a little'.
чуть не + verb: я чуть не упал = I nearly fell

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'рушить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to destroy', forming an aspectual pair with 'разрушать'.

examples.text: Ты разрушил мою семью своими фотографиями!
examples.trans: You destroyed my family with your photos!

examples.text: Ты разрушил такой прекрасный и сентиментальный момент!
examples.trans: You ruined such a wonderful and sentimental moment!

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to forgive', forming an aspectual pair with 'прощать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('excuse me, sorry') (imperative: прости / простите) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Conversational Russian particle ('please') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('you're welcome') (answer to thanks) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('here you are') (handing something over) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'щать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to forgive'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to say goodbye') (imperative 'прощайте' = farewell) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Тогда прощай, я должен срочно уйти.
examples.trans: Then farewell, I must urgently leave.
